obtained.how: open-access PDF from the publisher (PLOS ONE, CC BY)

bibliography.checked_against: Crossref and the article's first page
bibliography.note: Ali SE, Thoen E, Evensen Ø, Skaar I (2014) PLoS ONE 9(4): e91878, published 3 April 2014. Matches the entry.

claims.claim: Saprolegnia spreads from dead to live eggs within about three days even at 4–7 °C
claims.source_value: in the untreated controls, 3 days after infected dead eggs were introduced, hyphae grew out of them and colonized the surrounding live eggs; by day 5 the eggs had coalesced into one mould-covered mass; water 4–7 °C
claims.location: p. 4 (PDF p. 4), Results, 'Continuous treatment with BA prevents infection'; temperature p. 3, Methods, 'Effect of continuous exposure to BA'
claims.quote: 3 days after introduction of the infected, dead egg, the hyphae started growing out
claims.conditions: laboratory; eyed Atlantic salmon eggs in a single layer in close contact with three dead eggs per replicate of 27 ± 2 eggs; the dead eggs had been killed at 60 °C and pre-infected with Saprolegnia spores at 15 °C for 48 h; water 4–7 °C, pH 6.8–7.0
claims.note: The paper does not name the species: the rewrite should say 'in Atlantic salmon eggs in the laboratory'. The source dead eggs already carried hyphae (pre-infected at 15 °C), so the 3 days is the time for growth from an established focus to touching live eggs, not from spore arrival.

notes: The article is about boric acid as a treatment; the untreated controls give the spread rate. Day 5: 'eggs in the non-treated groups started to coalesce and formed a one-unit appearance of dead eggs, completely covered with Saprolegnia mycelium' (p. 4). No lake-fish species or field data.
